title: Deep Learning
subject: Deep Learning
summary: The architectures of modern deep learning and the mathematics behind them: convolutions, residual connections and normalization, recurrent and gated networks, attention as a mechanism, representation learning, the generative-model family (VAEs, GANs, normalizing flows, diffusion), training at scale, and deep learning in chemistry. The generative units are told through statistical mechanics: the ELBO is a variational free energy, flows obey the Liouville continuity equation, and diffusion models are Langevin dynamics with a learned score whose forward process is an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck SDE governed by a Fokker-Planck equation. The course ends with graph neural networks for molecules, AlphaFold and ML on spectra. Lessons teach the math and intuition; code lives in the optional PyTorch capstone.

units.title: Convolutional Networks
units.summary: Convolution as a weight-sharing, translation-equivariant linear layer: 1-D and 2-D kernels, channels, receptive fields, pooling, the gradient of a convolution and upsampling to the U-Net; the chemist's hook is that smoothing and derivative filters on a spectrum are already fixed 1-D convolutions.

lessons.title: Invariance, Equivariance and Why Convolution
objectives: Define translation invariance f(Tx) = f(x) and equivariance f(Tx) = T f(x), and decide which one image classification, object detection and segmentation each need.
Explain how locality and weight sharing turn a fully connected layer into a convolutional layer, and why this inductive bias suits images and spectra.
Count and compare the parameters of a fully connected layer and a 3x3 convolutional layer mapping a 64x64 image to a 64x64 feature map.

lectures.title: Lecture Collection | Convolutional Neural Networks for Visual Recognition (Spring 2017)

demoIdeas: Shift a drawing of a benzene ring across the image and watch a convolutional feature map shift with it (equivariance) while a global-max-pooled output stays fixed (invariance).

lessons.title: 1-D Convolution: Kernels, Stride, Padding and Dilation
objectives: Compute by hand the output of a 1-D convolution for a given kernel, stride, zero padding and dilation, and apply the output-length formula.
Distinguish convolution from cross-correlation and explain why deep-learning 'convolution' layers compute cross-correlation without loss of generality.
Recognise moving-average and Savitzky-Golay smoothing and finite-difference derivatives of an IR or UV-vis spectrum as fixed 1-D convolution kernels.
demoIdeas: Slide a 3-, 5- or 7-point kernel along a noisy IR spectrum; switch between smoothing and first-derivative kernels and change stride and dilation to see the output length and peak shapes change.

lessons.title: 2-D Convolution, Channels and 1x1 Convolutions
objectives: Compute the output shape and parameter count of a 2-D convolutional layer with C_in input channels, C_out output channels, a KxK kernel, stride and padding.
Explain a multi-channel convolution as each output channel summing 2-D correlations over all input channels, and a 1x1 convolution as a per-pixel linear map across channels.
Hand-design 3x3 kernels for blurring and for horizontal and vertical edge detection, and predict their feature maps on a simple image.

readings.title: Variants of the Basic Convolution Function

demoIdeas: Slide a user-editable 3x3 kernel over a grayscale image (a TLC plate photo) and watch the feature map fill in pixel by pixel; presets for blur, Sobel-x and Sobel-y.

lessons.title: Receptive Fields, Pooling and Downsampling
objectives: Compute the receptive field of a unit after a stack of convolution, stride and pooling layers.
Compare max pooling, average pooling and strided convolution as downsampling operations, and state the local invariance each provides.
Explain why two stacked 3x3 layers are preferred to one 5x5 layer (same receptive field, fewer parameters, an extra nonlinearity).
demoIdeas: Click a unit in a deep layer of a toy CNN and highlight its receptive field in the input image as layers are added and kernel sizes and strides change.

lessons.title: Backpropagation Through a Convolution
objectives: Derive the gradient of the loss with respect to a 1-D kernel as the cross-correlation of the layer input with the upstream gradient.
Derive the gradient with respect to the layer input as a full convolution of the upstream gradient with the flipped kernel, and check both on a 5-sample example.
Explain why weight sharing makes each kernel weight's gradient a sum over all positions.

readings.title: Variants of the Basic Convolution Function

demoIdeas: Step through the forward and backward pass of a 1-D convolution on a 6-sample signal, with arrows showing which inputs and upstream gradients feed each weight gradient.

lessons.title: Upsampling, Transposed Convolution and the U-Net
objectives: Write a strided convolution as a banded matrix and explain transposed convolution as multiplication by its transpose; compute the output size of a transposed convolution.
Describe the U-Net encoder-decoder with skip connections, explain why it suits dense per-pixel prediction, and note that it is the standard denoising network in diffusion models (Unit 8).
demoIdeas: Toggle between a strided convolution's banded matrix and its transpose to see a 4-sample signal upsampled to 8, with the checkerboard overlap pattern visible.

lessons.title: Classic CNN Architectures and What Filters Learn
objectives: Trace the progression LeNet to AlexNet to VGG in depth, kernel size, ReLU, dropout and data augmentation, and compute the parameter count of a VGG-style block.
Explain how first-layer filters (edges, colour blobs) and deeper features (textures, object parts) are visualised, and what a gradient saliency map does and does not show.
demoIdeas: Pick a unit in a small trained CNN and view its top-activating image patches next to a gradient saliency map overlaid on the input.

units.title: Residual Networks and Normalization
units.summary: Why very deep plain networks are hard to optimise and how residual connections and normalization layers restore signal propagation; the physics hook is that a residual block is one forward-Euler step of an ODE, like a step of a molecular-dynamics integrator.

lessons.title: Why Deep Plain Networks Are Hard to Train
objectives: Explain the degradation problem: deeper plain networks can have higher training error than shallower ones, so the obstacle is optimisation, not overfitting.
Describe shattered gradients, where gradients at nearby inputs become uncorrelated as depth grows, and relate it to the variance-propagation analysis of initialization from A2.
demoIdeas: Plot a deep plain network's gradient with respect to a 1-D input as a depth slider goes from 2 to 50 and watch it turn from smooth to noise; toggle residual connections to restore it.

lessons.title: Residual Connections and the Ensemble-of-Paths View
objectives: Write a residual block h_{k+1} = h_k + f_k(h_k) and expand a stack of three blocks into a sum over 2^3 paths of different lengths.
Show from the Jacobian product that the identity path gives the gradient a direct route through the network.
Interpret a residual network as forward-Euler integration of dh/dt = f(h, t) (the neural-ODE view), the same discretisation as integrating equations of motion in molecular dynamics.
demoIdeas: Watch 2-D points flow through a 20-block residual network trained to separate two spirals, each block drawn as a small Euler step along a vector field.

lessons.title: Variance Growth in Residual Networks
objectives: Show that adding residual branches makes the activation variance grow with depth (roughly doubling per block under He initialization).
Explain the two standard fixes: scaling the residual branches and placing normalization inside each block.
demoIdeas: Histogram activations block by block in a randomly initialized residual network; slide a branch-scale factor and toggle normalization to keep the variance flat.

lessons.title: Normalization Layers: Batch, Layer and Group Norm
objectives: Recall batch normalization from A2 and contrast batch, layer, instance and group normalization by which axes of an N x C x H x W tensor the mean and variance are computed over.
Explain why batch norm misbehaves with small batches and variable-length sequences and why transformers use layer norm instead.
Compare pre-norm and post-norm placement in a residual block and explain why pre-norm keeps the identity path clean.
demoIdeas: Highlight the cells of an N x C x H x W tensor that share one mean and variance under batch, layer, instance and group norm, and see the normalized values for a toy batch.

lessons.title: Common Residual Architectures and Why They Work
objectives: Describe the ResNet bottleneck block (1x1, 3x3, 1x1) and compare its parameter count with a basic two-layer block.
Compare ResNet (addition), DenseNet (concatenation) and U-Net/hourglass skip connections.
Summarise the loss-landscape evidence that residual connections smooth the optimisation landscape.

readings.title: Why do nets with residual connections perform so well?

demoIdeas: Compare 2-D slices of the loss landscape of a deep network with and without skip connections as interactive contour plots.

units.title: Recurrent Networks, LSTMs and GRUs
units.summary: Sequence models that share parameters across time: unfolding, backpropagation through time, the eigenvalue story behind vanishing and exploding gradients (diagonalisation from M3), and the gated LSTM and GRU cells that fix it; kinetic traces and chromatograms are the chemist's sequences.

lessons.title: Unfolding Computation in Time: the Simple RNN
objectives: Write the simple RNN update h_t = tanh(W h_{t-1} + U x_t + b) and draw its unfolded computational graph for T steps.
Contrast parameter sharing across time in an RNN with sharing across positions in a 1-D convolution (unbounded vs finite memory).
Classify sequence tasks as many-to-one, many-to-many or sequence-to-sequence and give a chemistry example of each (e.g. a kinetic trace to a rate constant).

lectures.title: Lecture 2: Deep Sequence Modeling (RNNs, LSTMs, attention)

demoIdeas: Feed a sequence one symbol at a time into a 2-unit RNN and watch the hidden state trace a trajectory in the plane.

lessons.title: Backpropagation Through Time
objectives: Derive the BPTT gradient of the loss with respect to the recurrent matrix W as a sum over time steps of products of Jacobians.
Explain truncated BPTT and teacher forcing and their trade-offs.

readings.title: Computing the Gradient in a Recurrent Neural Network
Teacher Forcing and Networks with Output Recurrence

demoIdeas: Animate the backward pass through an unrolled RNN, colouring each time step by the size of its contribution to the gradient.

lessons.title: Vanishing and Exploding Gradients: the Eigenvalue Story
objectives: Show that for a linear RNN the gradient across k steps scales as W^k, so the eigenvalues of W decide vanishing (|lambda| < 1) or exploding (|lambda| > 1) gradients, using diagonalisation from M3.
Explain gradient-norm clipping and why it cures explosion but not vanishing.
Explain why a simple RNN struggles to learn a dependency 50 steps back.
demoIdeas: Set the eigenvalues of a 2x2 recurrent matrix with sliders and watch the gradient norm over 100 time steps vanish, stay flat or explode on a log plot; toggle clipping.

lessons.title: Gated Cells: LSTM and GRU
objectives: Write the LSTM equations (forget, input and output gates and the cell state) and explain how the additive cell update gives a near-identity gradient path.
Write the GRU equations and contrast them with the LSTM (merged gates, no separate cell state).
Relate the LSTM cell-state path to the residual connection of Unit 2.

readings.title: The Long Short-Term Memory and Other Gated RNNs
Leaky Units and Other Strategies for Multiple Time Scales

demoIdeas: Open or close each LSTM gate on a toy memory task and watch the cell state carry or forget a stored bit across 40 time steps.

lessons.title: Bidirectional and Seq2seq Models; Dilated Convolutions for Sequences
objectives: Describe bidirectional RNNs and encoder-decoder sequence-to-sequence models, and identify the fixed-length context vector as the bottleneck that attention removes.
Explain how stacked dilated causal 1-D convolutions (WaveNet) reach a receptive field exponential in depth, and compare them with RNNs for parallel training.

lectures.source: Andrej Karpathy, Neural Networks: Zero to Hero
lectures.title: Building makemore Part 5: Building a WaveNet

demoIdeas: Stack dilated causal convolutions with dilations 1, 2, 4, 8 and highlight which past time steps feed the current output.

units.title: Attention as a Mechanism
units.summary: Attention as a differentiable, content-based lookup: queries, keys and values, scaled dot-product self-attention (its softmax is a Boltzmann distribution over keys), masking, positional information and multiple heads; the full transformer and language models are A4's subject.

lessons.title: Attention as Soft Dictionary Lookup
objectives: Explain additive (Bahdanau) attention in a seq2seq model as alignment weights over encoder states that replace the fixed context vector.
Interpret attention as a soft key-value lookup, and its softmax weights as a Boltzmann distribution over keys with scores as negative energies and a temperature.

readings.title: Using an Attention Mechanism and Aligning Pieces of Data

lectures.title: Lecture 2: Deep Sequence Modeling (RNNs, LSTMs, attention)

demoIdeas: Drag a query vector and watch softmax attention weights over 8 key vectors sharpen or flatten as the temperature is lowered or raised.

lessons.title: Scaled Dot-Product Self-Attention
objectives: Compute self-attention by hand for 3 tokens with given W_q, W_k, W_v: Q, K, V, the score matrix, the row-wise softmax and the output.
Explain the 1/sqrt(d_k) scaling: with unit-variance entries a dot product has variance d_k, which would saturate the softmax.
Show that self-attention is permutation-equivariant and costs O(N^2 d) for N tokens.

lectures.source: Andrej Karpathy, Neural Networks: Zero to Hero
lectures.title: Let's build GPT: from scratch, in code, spelled out.

demoIdeas: Show the N x N attention matrix as a heatmap for a short sentence or SMILES string and let the learner edit token embeddings to see the weights change.

lessons.title: Masking, Positional Encodings and Multi-Head Attention
objectives: Explain why self-attention needs positional information and compute sinusoidal positional encodings for small positions.
Apply a causal mask (minus infinity above the diagonal) and explain its role in autoregressive generation.
Describe multi-head attention as several lower-dimensional attentions run in parallel and concatenated, and count its parameters.
demoIdeas: Toggle a causal mask on an attention heatmap and compare 4 heads side by side, each attending to different relative positions.

lessons.title: The Transformer Block and Attention Beyond Text
objectives: Assemble a transformer block (multi-head attention and an MLP, each wrapped in a residual connection with layer norm) and trace tensor shapes through it.
Explain how a vision transformer turns an image into a sequence of patches, and compare its inductive bias with a CNN's.
Recognise self-attention as message passing on a fully connected graph (a preview of graph neural networks in Unit 10).
demoIdeas: Cut an image into 16x16 patches, lay them out as a token sequence, and show one patch's attention map over all the others.

units.title: Representation Learning and Embeddings
units.summary: What networks learn in their hidden layers: distributed representations and the manifold hypothesis, autoencoders and their link to PCA, denoising autoencoders that secretly estimate the score of the data density, transfer learning, and contrastive embeddings; hand-made molecular fingerprints versus learned embeddings is the chemist's hook.

lessons.title: Distributed Representations and the Manifold Hypothesis
objectives: Contrast local (one-hot) and distributed representations and explain how n binary features can separate 2^n regions.
State the manifold hypothesis and explain why molecular conformations and spectra lie near low-dimensional manifolds in high-dimensional spaces.
Compare a hand-crafted molecular fingerprint (e.g. ECFP) with a learned embedding by what each captures and how it is obtained.
demoIdeas: Project a learned embedding of small molecules to 2-D and hover over points to see structures cluster by functional group.

lessons.title: Autoencoders and Their Link to PCA
objectives: Write the autoencoder objective and explain the role of the bottleneck in an undercomplete autoencoder.
Show that a linear autoencoder trained with squared error spans the same subspace as PCA (the SVD from M3 and A1).
Explain what nonlinear autoencoders add and why an overcomplete autoencoder needs regularisation to avoid learning the identity.
demoIdeas: Train a 2-unit-bottleneck autoencoder on a curved 3-D point cloud and compare its 2-D code with the PCA projection.

lessons.title: Denoising Autoencoders Estimate the Score
objectives: Write the denoising autoencoder objective: corrupt x with Gaussian noise and train the network to reconstruct the clean x.
Use Tweedie's formula to show that the optimal denoiser's correction r(x~) - x~ equals sigma^2 times the score grad log p_sigma(x~) of the noised density.
Explain why this result is the seed of score-based diffusion models (Unit 8).
demoIdeas: Draw the vector field r(x~) - x~ learned by a denoising autoencoder on a 2-D ring of points and compare it with the true score arrows at several noise levels.

lessons.title: Transfer Learning, Pretraining and Fine-Tuning
objectives: Explain why features learned on a large task transfer, and distinguish linear probing, fine-tuning and training from scratch.
Choose and justify a transfer strategy for a small labelled chemistry data set (e.g. 500 measured solubilities) given a model pretrained on millions of unlabelled molecules.
demoIdeas: Slide the size of the labelled training set and compare learning curves for from-scratch, linear-probe and fine-tuned models.

lessons.title: Self-Supervised and Contrastive Embeddings
objectives: Write the InfoNCE loss and recognise it as softmax cross-entropy over one positive and many negatives at a temperature tau.
Explain how the choice of positive pairs (two augmentations of an image, two SMILES of one molecule, a structure and its spectrum CLIP-style) decides what the embedding becomes invariant to.
Relate InfoNCE to noise-contrastive estimation.
demoIdeas: Watch embeddings on a unit circle as contrastive training pulls positive pairs together and pushes negatives apart, with a temperature slider.

units.title: Generative Models I: Latent Variables, VAEs and GANs
units.summary: How to judge a generative model, latent-variable models and the ELBO (a variational free energy with the same structure as the Gibbs-Bogoliubov bound of statistical mechanics), variational autoencoders and the reparameterization trick, and adversarial training with its Jensen-Shannon and Wasserstein views.

lessons.title: What Makes a Good Generative Model?
objectives: Sort VAEs, GANs, normalizing flows and diffusion models by whether they give an exact likelihood, a bound or none, and by sampling speed.
Explain the evaluation measures (test log-likelihood, Inception score, Frechet Inception distance) and why likelihood and sample quality can disagree.

readings.title: What makes a good generative model?

lectures.title: Lecture 4: Deep Generative Modeling (autoencoders, VAEs, GANs, diffusion)
Lecture 13 | Generative Models (in the Spring 2017 lecture collection)

demoIdeas: Compare samples from four toy generators on a 2-D two-moons data set alongside their log-likelihood and an FID-like score.

lessons.title: Latent Variable Models and the Marginal Likelihood
objectives: Write a latent variable model p(x) = integral of p(x|z) p(z) dz and show that a Gaussian mixture is its discrete special case.
Explain why the marginal likelihood is intractable for a neural-network decoder, and compare this integral with a partition function.
demoIdeas: Move through a 1-D latent space and watch the decoder's output density over 2-D data, with the marginal p(x) built from all z overlaid.

lessons.title: The Evidence Lower Bound as a Free Energy
objectives: Derive the ELBO with Jensen's inequality and show that log p(x) minus the ELBO equals KL(q(z|x) || p(z|x)).
Rewrite the negative ELBO as 'energy minus entropy' and identify it with a variational Helmholtz free energy, which upper-bounds -kT log Z exactly as in the Gibbs-Bogoliubov inequality.
Decompose the ELBO into a reconstruction term and a KL-to-prior term and explain what each rewards.
demoIdeas: Fit a Gaussian q(z) to a bimodal posterior by sliding its mean and width, and watch the ELBO, the KL gap and log p(x) as three bars.

lessons.title: The Variational Autoencoder and the Reparameterization Trick
objectives: Assemble a VAE: an encoder giving the mean and variance of q(z|x), a decoder p(x|z), and the closed-form KL term to a standard normal prior.
Explain why sampling blocks gradients and how z = mu + sigma * epsilon moves the randomness off the gradient path.
Explain posterior collapse and blurry samples as typical VAE failure modes.
demoIdeas: Drag a point through the 2-D latent space of a VAE trained on handwritten digits and decode it live.

lessons.title: Generative Adversarial Networks: the Minimax Game
objectives: Write the GAN minimax objective and derive the optimal discriminator D*(x) = p_data(x) / (p_data(x) + p_g(x)).
Show that against D* the generator minimises 2 JS(p_data || p_g) - log 4.
Explain the non-saturating generator loss and why it is used in practice.
demoIdeas: Watch a 1-D generator's density and the discriminator's decision curve evolve step by step as the two train against each other.

lessons.title: GAN Training Pathologies and the Wasserstein Distance
objectives: Explain mode collapse and vanishing discriminator gradients when the data and generated distributions have nearly disjoint support.
Define the Wasserstein (earth mover's) distance, state its Kantorovich-Rubinstein dual form, and explain why a WGAN critic must be 1-Lipschitz.
demoIdeas: Train a GAN on a ring of 8 Gaussians and watch mode collapse happen; switch to a Wasserstein loss and compare how many modes are covered.

units.title: Generative Models II: Normalizing Flows
units.summary: Exact-likelihood generative models built from invertible maps: the change-of-variables formula, coupling layers with cheap Jacobian determinants, and continuous flows whose density obeys the continuity (Liouville) equation; Boltzmann generators that sample molecular conformations are the chemist's hook.

lessons.title: Change of Variables and the Jacobian Determinant
objectives: Derive the 1-D change-of-variables formula and apply it to a monotone map of a standard normal.
Generalise to D dimensions with the Jacobian determinant and explain why its O(D^3) cost drives the design of flow layers.
Write the exact negative log-likelihood training objective of a flow built from K layers.
demoIdeas: Drag the control points of a monotone 1-D spline and watch a standard normal stretch into a bimodal density, with |df/dz| shaded.

lessons.title: Invertible Layers: Coupling Flows and Boltzmann Generators
objectives: Construct an affine coupling layer, show that its Jacobian is triangular, and compute its log-determinant as a sum of log-scales.
Explain why alternating which half is transformed (and adding permutations) lets a stack of couplings model arbitrary dependencies.
Describe Boltzmann generators: flows trained against an energy function U(x) to draw molecular configurations with Boltzmann weights exp(-U/kT), reweighted for exactness.
demoIdeas: Apply affine coupling layers one at a time to a 2-D Gaussian and watch it deform into two moons, with each layer's log-determinant displayed.

lessons.title: Continuous Flows and the Continuity Equation
objectives: Write a continuous normalizing flow dx/dt = v(x, t) and derive the instantaneous change of log-density d log p/dt = -div v.
Recognise the continuity equation dp/dt + div(p v) = 0 as probability conservation, the Liouville equation of classical and statistical mechanics.
Explain how a continuous flow is the infinite-depth limit of the residual network of Unit 2.

lectures.title: Lecture 1: Flow and Diffusion Models (course page with slides, notes and recordings)

demoIdeas: Draw a time-dependent 2-D velocity field and watch a particle cloud and its density colouring flow from a Gaussian to a target shape, with divergence shown as compression or expansion.

units.title: Diffusion Models, Score Matching and Langevin Dynamics
units.summary: Diffusion models through statistical mechanics: Langevin dynamics samples a Boltzmann distribution from its score (the force over kT, no partition function needed), the forward noising process is an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck SDE whose density obeys a Fokker-Planck equation, a network learns the score by denoising score matching, and sampling runs the dynamics backwards; flow matching and guidance complete the picture (the generative core of AlphaFold 3 and molecular conformer generators).

lessons.title: Score Functions and Langevin Dynamics
objectives: Define the score grad_x log p(x) and show that for a Boltzmann density p proportional to exp(-U/kT) it equals the force -grad U / kT, independent of the partition function Z.
Write the overdamped Langevin update and explain why its stationary distribution is p(x), connecting it to Brownian dynamics of a molecule in solution.
Explain why Langevin sampling with an estimated score fails in low-density regions and how annealing over noise levels fixes it.

lectures.source: MIT 6.S184 (2026): Introduction to Flow Matching and Diffusion Models
lectures.title: Lecture 3-A: Score Functions and Score Matching (course page with slides, notes and recordings)

demoIdeas: Run Langevin dynamics on a 2-D double-well potential: adjust temperature and step size and watch the particle histogram converge to the Boltzmann distribution.

lessons.title: The Forward Process: Noising Data into a Gaussian
objectives: Write the forward step q(x_t | x_{t-1}) = N(sqrt(1 - beta_t) x_{t-1}, beta_t I) and derive the closed-form marginal q(x_t | x_0) in terms of alpha-bar_t.
Explain why the variance-preserving scaling sends any data distribution to N(0, I), and compare linear and cosine noise schedules.

lectures.title: Lecture 4: Deep Generative Modeling (autoencoders, VAEs, GANs, diffusion)

demoIdeas: Scrub a time slider and watch a 2-D point cloud (a spiral, or the atom positions of a small molecule) dissolve into Gaussian noise under a chosen beta schedule.

lessons.title: The SDE and Fokker-Planck View
objectives: Write the continuous-time forward process as the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck SDE dx = -1/2 beta(t) x dt + sqrt(beta(t)) dW and identify it as Brownian motion in a harmonic well.
Write the Fokker-Planck equation for this SDE and show that N(0, I) is its stationary solution.
State the reverse-time SDE (Anderson) and identify the score of p_t as the only unknown needed to run diffusion backwards.

lectures.source: MIT 6.S184 (2026): Introduction to Flow Matching and Diffusion Models
lectures.title: Lecture 1: Flow and Diffusion Models (SDEs; course page with slides, notes and recordings)

demoIdeas: Evolve a bimodal 1-D density under the forward Fokker-Planck equation as a p(x, t) heat map beside a histogram of simulated SDE particles.

lessons.title: Score Matching and Denoising Score Matching
objectives: Write the explicit score-matching objective, explain why it needs the unknown true score, and state Hyvarinen's integration-by-parts form with the trace of the score's Jacobian.
Derive denoising score matching: the score of the Gaussian perturbation kernel, -(x~ - x)/sigma^2, is a valid regression target, so the network learns grad log p_sigma.
Connect denoising score matching to the denoising autoencoder of Unit 5 and to noise prediction via s_theta(x_t, t) = -epsilon_theta(x_t, t) / sqrt(1 - alpha-bar_t).
demoIdeas: Train a tiny score network on a 2-D mixture of Gaussians and overlay its learned score arrows on the true ones at several noise levels sigma.

lessons.title: The Reverse Process and the DDPM Loss
objectives: Derive the Gaussian posterior q(x_{t-1} | x_t, x_0) and explain why the learned reverse step p_theta(x_{t-1} | x_t) is taken to be Gaussian.
Show how the diffusion ELBO reduces to a sum of KL divergences between Gaussians and, after reparameterising the mean, to the simple noise-prediction loss.
demoIdeas: Pick a time step t to see a noisy point x_t, the true noise, a model's predicted noise and the loss; scrub t to find which steps are hardest.

lessons.title: Sampling: Ancestral Steps, the Reverse SDE and the Probability-Flow ODE
objectives: Write the DDPM ancestral sampling step and carry out one step by hand.
Derive the probability-flow ODE that shares the SDE's marginals, and explain deterministic (DDIM-style) sampling and its speed-quality trade-off.
Identify the probability-flow ODE as a continuous normalizing flow (Unit 7) whose velocity field is built from the score.
demoIdeas: Run reverse diffusion on a 2-D point cloud: Gaussian noise denoises into a spiral step by step; toggle stochastic (SDE) versus deterministic (ODE) sampling and change the number of steps.

lessons.title: Flow Matching
objectives: Define a probability path from noise to data and the conditional velocity field for the straight-line path x_t = (1 - t) x_0 + t x_1.
Write the conditional flow-matching loss and explain why regressing the conditional velocity yields the marginal velocity field.
Compare flow matching with diffusion (straighter paths, fewer sampling steps) and note that both learn the velocity field of a continuity equation.

lectures.title: Lecture 2: Flow Matching (course page with slides, notes and recordings)

demoIdeas: Compare particle trajectories from noise to a two-moons distribution under a diffusion path and a straight flow-matching path, counting the ODE steps each needs.

lessons.title: Conditional Generation and Guidance
objectives: Apply Bayes' rule to scores, grad log p(x|y) = grad log p(x) + grad log p(y|x), to derive classifier guidance.
Derive classifier-free guidance as an extrapolation between conditional and unconditional noise estimates and explain the fidelity-diversity trade-off of the guidance scale w.
Describe conditional diffusion in chemistry: generating 3-D conformers from a molecular graph, or ligand poses inside a protein pocket.

units.title: Training at Scale
units.summary: The engineering mathematics of training large networks: minibatch size and gradient noise, data pipelines, floating-point formats and mixed precision, data and model parallelism and memory budgets, and a practical methodology for debugging a training run.

lessons.title: Minibatches, Batch Size and Gradient Noise
objectives: Show that the minibatch gradient is an unbiased estimator whose variance falls as 1/B, and explain the linear learning-rate scaling rule and where it breaks down.
Describe a data pipeline (shuffling, batching, prefetching, on-the-fly augmentation) and explain why GPU utilisation depends on it.

lectures.title: Secrets to Massively Parallel Training (guest lecture, Mathias Lechner, Liquid AI)

demoIdeas: Show SGD trajectories on a 2-D loss surface for batch sizes 1, 16 and 256, with a gradient-noise cloud drawn around each step.

lessons.title: Floating Point and Mixed Precision
objectives: Compare fp32, fp16 and bf16 by exponent and mantissa bits, dynamic range and machine epsilon.
Explain mixed-precision training (low-precision matrix multiplies, fp32 master weights and accumulation) and why loss scaling prevents fp16 gradient underflow.
Apply the log-sum-exp trick to compute softmax and cross-entropy stably.
keyEquations: \log\sum_i e^{x_i} = m + \log\sum_i e^{x_i - m},\quad m = \max_i x_i
demoIdeas: Type a number to see its bit pattern and rounding error in fp32, fp16 and bf16; slide a loss scale and watch small gradients survive or underflow to zero.

lessons.title: Data Parallelism, Model Parallelism and Memory
objectives: Estimate the memory of a training run (weights, gradients, Adam moments, activations) for a given parameter count and precision.
Contrast data parallelism (all-reduce of gradients) with model and pipeline parallelism, and explain gradient accumulation and activation checkpointing as memory-for-compute trades.
keyEquations: M \approx (4 + 4 + 8)\,P\ \text{bytes} + M_{act}\quad(\text{fp32 weights, gradients, Adam moments})
demoIdeas: A stacked-bar memory calculator: enter parameter count, batch size and precision and see GPU memory split into weights, gradients, optimizer states and activations, with toggles for checkpointing and sharding.

lessons.title: Practical Methodology: Debugging a Training Run
objectives: Apply a debugging checklist: overfit a single batch, check the initial loss (about log C for C classes), and monitor gradient norms and activation statistics.
Run a learning-rate range test and read training and validation curves to diagnose under- versus overfitting.
Choose a baseline and a hyperparameter search strategy, and explain why random search beats grid search.
demoIdeas: Pick a broken training run from a menu (learning rate too high, shuffled labels, missing input normalization) and diagnose it from its loss and gradient-norm curves.

units.title: Deep Learning in Science: Molecules, Proteins and Spectra
units.summary: Where the chemist's own data meet the course: molecules as graphs, message passing (the adjacency matrix of a conjugated system is the Hueckel Hamiltonian), molecular property prediction, symmetry-aware 3-D networks for energies and forces, AlphaFold's architecture, and deep learning on IR, NMR and mass spectra.

lessons.title: Molecules as Graphs
objectives: Encode a molecule as a graph with node features (element, formal charge, hybridisation), edge features (bond order) and an adjacency matrix, and write these out for ethanol.
Explain why a graph model must be permutation-invariant for graph-level outputs and permutation-equivariant for node-level outputs, and show that relabelling atoms maps A to P A P^T.
Classify graph-, node- and edge-level tasks with chemistry examples (solubility, partial charges, bond reactivity).

readings.title: Graph neural networks, tasks, and loss functions

lectures.title: AI for Science (guest lecture, Chris Bishop, Microsoft)

demoIdeas: Draw a small molecule and see its adjacency and node-feature matrices update; relabel atoms and watch rows and columns permute together.

lessons.title: Message Passing and Graph Convolutions
objectives: Write a graph-convolution layer with self-loops and symmetric degree normalisation, compute one layer by hand for a 4-atom molecule, and note that the adjacency matrix of a conjugated system is, up to alpha and beta, its Hueckel Hamiltonian.
Generalise to message passing (message, aggregate, update) and explain why sum, mean or max aggregation preserves permutation equivariance.
Explain how K layers give each atom a K-bond neighbourhood, and the over-smoothing problem.
demoIdeas: Step message passing on a drawn molecule: each atom's colour mixes its neighbours' colours layer by layer, showing the receptive field grow one bond at a time.

lessons.title: Molecular Property Prediction
objectives: Build a graph-level model (message passing, a permutation-invariant readout, an MLP head) and explain why sum readout suits extensive properties such as energies and mean readout suits intensive ones.
Explain scaffold versus random splits and why random splits overestimate performance on new chemistry.
Compare a GNN with a fingerprint-plus-MLP baseline and state when each tends to win as data size changes.
demoIdeas: Compare test error under random and scaffold splits for a toy solubility model, with held-out molecules coloured by scaffold.

lessons.title: Geometry and Symmetry: Invariant and Equivariant 3-D Networks
objectives: Explain why 3-D molecular models should be invariant (energies) or equivariant (forces, dipoles) under rotations, translations and reflections, and show that F = -grad E inherits equivariance from an invariant E.

Describe how distance-based models (SchNet-style radial-basis features) achieve invariance and how equivariant networks carry vector features, and why built-in symmetry improves the data efficiency of machine-learned force fields.
demoIdeas: Rotate a water molecule in 3-D and compare the outputs of an invariant energy model (unchanged), an equivariant force model (arrows rotate with it) and a plain MLP on raw coordinates (changes arbitrarily).

lessons.title: AlphaFold: Deep Learning for Protein Structure
objectives: Describe the AlphaFold 2 pipeline: MSA and pair representations, the Evoformer's row/column attention and triangle updates, and the structure module that outputs 3-D coordinates with pLDDT confidence.
Explain why co-evolution in a multiple sequence alignment carries residue-contact information, and what consistency of pairwise distances the triangle updates encourage.
Explain how AlphaFold 3 replaces the structure module with a diffusion module that generates all-atom complexes, connecting to Unit 8.
demoIdeas: Show a contact map estimated from a toy MSA's covariance next to the protein's 3-D structure; click a contact to highlight the residue pair in 3-D.

lessons.title: Deep Learning on Spectra
objectives: Choose input representations for IR, NMR and mass spectra (binned vectors, peak lists as sets, 2-D NMR as images) and match each to an architecture (1-D CNN, set model or transformer, 2-D CNN).

Distinguish the forward problem (structure to spectrum, e.g. GNN-predicted NMR shifts) from the inverse problem (spectrum to structure or functional groups), and explain why the inverse is ill-posed and often framed as retrieval or conditional generation.
Design physically sensible augmentations (small peak shifts, baseline drift, noise, intensity scaling) and justify each from how the spectrum is measured.
demoIdeas: Feed a simulated IR spectrum through a 1-D CNN functional-group classifier; apply augmentations with sliders and watch a saliency trace highlight the C=O and O-H regions.

exams.title: A3 Midterm: Convolutions, Residual Networks, Recurrence, Attention and Representations

project.title: From Convolutions to Diffusion: a CNN and a Small Diffusion Model in PyTorch
project.summary: Build two models from scratch in PyTorch. First a residual CNN with batch norm that classifies images (Fashion-MNIST) or simulated IR spectra by functional group; then a small denoising diffusion model that learns a 2-D point cloud and finally MNIST digits, sampled three ways (DDPM, a deterministic probability-flow sampler, and annealed Langevin dynamics with the learned score) to make the stat-mech picture concrete.
goals: Implement and train a residual CNN with batch normalization in PyTorch, and inspect its filters and saliency maps.
Implement the diffusion forward process, the noise-prediction training loop and the ancestral sampler.
Verify the score connection by sampling the trained model with annealed Langevin dynamics and a probability-flow ODE.
Practise training-at-scale habits: data loaders, mixed precision, checkpoints and loss-curve debugging.
steps: Set up PyTorch (CPU or a consumer GPU) and write a Dataset/DataLoader for Fashion-MNIST or a simulated IR-spectrum set (Lorentzian peaks per functional group plus noise and baseline); plot a batch.
Build a small CNN (conv-BN-ReLU blocks, pooling, linear head), confirm it can overfit one batch, then train with Adam and plot training and validation curves.
Add residual blocks, compare accuracy and gradient norms with the plain network, and visualise first-layer filters and a saliency map.
Turn on mixed precision (torch.autocast with a gradient scaler) and gradient accumulation and measure the speed and memory differences.
Implement the forward noising process with a linear or cosine beta schedule on a 2-D Swiss roll or two-moons set and animate x_t over t.
Train a small MLP noise predictor epsilon_theta(x_t, t) with a sinusoidal time embedding using the simple noise-prediction loss.
Implement DDPM ancestral sampling and a deterministic DDIM/probability-flow sampler; compare samples against the number of steps.
Convert epsilon_theta into a score, sample with annealed Langevin dynamics, and plot the learned score field against the true one at several noise levels.
Scale up: train a small U-Net diffusion model on MNIST and show a grid of generated digits, optionally with classifier-free guidance on the digit label.
